newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon changes figures in Gulf illness probe.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon changes figures in Gulf illness probe.

text.p: The Pentagon on Thursday raised to 27,000 from 21,000 its estimate of the maximum number of U.S. Gulf War troops who could have been in a 32-mile 50 km radius of an Iraqi chemical arms dump when it was destroyed in 1991.

The initial estimate had been made by the Defence Department earlier this year in attempts to determine how many troops could have been exposed to chemical agents when the Kamisiyah ammo dump was blown up in March 1991.

But the Pentagon also cautioned on Thursday that new talks with Gulf veterans indicated only 13,000 U.S. soldiers were inside the circle around Kamisiyah in southern Iraq on March 10 when chemical rockets were blown up in an open pit.
Chemical weapons were also blown up at Kamisiyah earlier in March of that year but did not cause a large cloud of smoke and gas like the one that drifted away from the March 10 blast.

Thousands of Gulf veterans have complained of ills ranging from joint aches to loss of memory, but no cause has been found for the complaints. Congress has accused the Pentagon and White House of failure to properly investigate the matter.

Bernard Rostker, the Pentagon's special assistant for Gulf War illnesses, said on Thursday that the department had now refined its earlier estimate that perhaps 21,000 troops from the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions and the 24th Infantry Division were in the circle around Kamisiyah in March 1991.

He said a recent conference involving Pentagon officials and Gulf War veterans had determined that as many as 27,000 U.S. troops were in the zone at one time or another in March, although not necessarily all at once.
"Twenty-seven thousand were in the Kamisiyah area," he said, cautioning that the figure could have been smaller on any given day.
"It's possible somebody came in on the 6th and left on 9th," Rostker told reporters.

The Pentagon and Central Intelligence Agency are currently developing a computer model of the cloud that may have contained Sarin nerve gas and drifted in one or several directions from Kamisiyah on March 10.
Rostker said results of that study are expected in July.

A congressional report on Monday criticised the Pentagon and a White House panel looking into the ills of Gulf War veterans, warning that Iraqi chemical and biological agents cannot yet be discounted as possible culprits.

The report by the General Accounting Office, the investigating arm of Congress, also said there was "substantial evidence" that fertiliser compounds used in the Gulf could be associated with problems similar to those of the veterans.
The report criticised the Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans Illnesses for virtually discounting any link between biological agents and troop complaints.
